title_en: GPT-6.1 Sol helps CodeRabbit strengthen security across complex codebases
excerpt_en: CodeRabbit uses GPT-6.1 Sol to investigate security risks across complex codebases. Its security agent helps developers review findings and proposed fixes.
content_en:
# GPT‑6.1 Sol helps CodeRabbit strengthen security across complex codebases

As AI accelerates software development, engineering and application-security teams need ways to investigate code changes and address vulnerabilities while keeping people in control. CodeRabbit is using <u>GPT‑6.1 Sol</u> as the primary model in its security agent to extend review beyond individual changes and help developers understand risks across complex codebases.

A pull request can affect shared libraries, dependencies and safeguards elsewhere in an application. GPT‑6.1 Sol helps CodeRabbit connect behavior across files and components to surface potential security issues. CodeRabbit’s review is independent of the agent that wrote the code and complements established scanners. Its system also uses other frontier models and security tooling.

During pull-request review, Sol helps analyze changes as developers work. In Deep Scan, it supports broader investigation across repositories, including dependencies and how components interact. CodeRabbit Secure extends that investigation to linked repositories, such as a shared authentication library, to help teams understand how a weakness could affect the wider system.

CodeRabbit reports using GPT‑6.1 Sol to flag security-related issues across thousands of repositories and organizations. These findings feed into the pull-request workflows developers already use to review and improve their code.

CodeRabbit Secure connects investigation to remediation. For user-selected findings, it can attempt exploit verification in an isolated sandbox without testing production systems. For supported issues, it can draft a pull request with a proposed fix for a person to review and approve.

This work shows how frontier reasoning can support software security: understanding risks beyond an individual change, helping validate findings and turning them into proposed fixes. Human reviewers remain responsible for deciding which changes to ship.

Learn more about GPT‑6.1 Sol <u>here</u>. Learn more about CodeRabbit Secure <u>here</u>(opens in a new window).

title: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt deal for AI chips, Elon Musk says
excerpt: Elon Musk said in an X post that SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to purchase GPUs.
title_en: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt deal for AI chips, Elon Musk says
excerpt_en: Elon Musk said in an X post that SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to purchase GPUs.
content_en:
SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy graphics processing units, or GPUs, used to power artificial intelligence systems.

In a post on X on Sunday, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said it had closed the financing, adding that the company was investment grade and generated revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket launch businesses.

In a follow-up post, he added that the financing primarily consisted of callable debt for graphics processing units, which are expected to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027.

In a regulatory filing Monday, SpaceX said it signed a binding commitment with an Apollo-managed entity for roughly $40 billion in GPU financing.

The financing underscores the AI boom's enormous capital requirements, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into advanced chips and data centers to support increasingly powerful AI models.

## SpaceX ramps up AI infrastructure spending

SpaceX has expanded aggressively into artificial intelligence this year, referring to the business as "Super Intelligence," or SI.

The segment has become the company's largest business unit, with third-quarter revenue surging ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million a year earlier, according to its latest earnings release.

Musk also said that debt markets have largely shut off access to financing for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers.

He predicted that more than 200 so-called neocloud companies, which provide cloud computing infrastructure designed for AI and machine-learning workloads, would face widespread failures and consolidation, with only a small number surviving.

title: ChatGPT’s expanding world of work
excerpt: Explore OpenAI Signals data on 165 work activities across nearly 100 countries, revealing how people use ChatGPT for work and how usage changes over time.
excerpt_en: Explore OpenAI Signals data on 165 work activities across nearly 100 countries, revealing how people use ChatGPT for work and how usage changes over time.
content_en:
# ChatGPT’s expanding world of work

OpenAI Economic Research releases data for researchers to explore questions on AI and labor more deeply.

Today, we are releasing <u>OpenAI Signals data that explores</u> 165 work activities across nearly 100 countries, revealing how consumers use ChatGPT for work. This data gives researchers a new way to study AI’s role in the economy, with new information on the work activities people bring to ChatGPT—from preparing instructional materials and developing marketing content to programming and analyzing business data.

Researchers can use this data to explore how ChatGPT use for work differs across countries, track changes over time, and match this data to other economic indicators. The release connects ChatGPT usage to 165 work activity categories called Intermediate Work Activities (IWAs). IWAs are commonly-used categories of tasks for the kinds of work people do across occupations. The data is represented quarterly, spanning a period from the first quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026.

Our new data draws on O\*NET, a standardized framework that groups occupation-specific tasks into broader categories of work activities shared across occupations. Using a common framework helps researchers compare ChatGPT use with other types of occupational and employment data.

The interactive chart below can be used to explore these work activities within a specific country over time, moving from broad activity groups to more specific activities. The data shows wide variation across countries in how people use ChatGPT for work.

Connecting this data to IWAs revealed that work-related use became less concentrated in the most common activities. That means that countries tended to specialize in their work over time, and different countries specialized in different types of work. These differences might reflect variation in the kind of work done across countries or varying access to AI tools. Exploring these questions is one example of many that researchers can pursue with this new data.

Connecting ChatGPT usage data with IWAs lets researchers compare ChatGPT messages with activities performed across U.S. jobs. The paired visualizations below compare how people use ChatGPT with the activities performed across U.S. jobs. This comparison shows the difference in how people use ChatGPT for work and the actual work being done in the U.S. economy. The two distributions differ substantially, largely because about 43% of the employment-weighted task mix for mapped U.S. occupations falls into Other IWAs, outside the individually reported categories. These include activities such as moving materials, operating vehicles, and maintaining health or medical records. These omitted categories did not meet our threshold for consistent representation in the original U.S. ChatGPT sample.

This release builds on OpenAI Signals, our ongoing effort to share evidence about how people use AI. The data covers work-related messages on individual ChatGPT plans and does not include enterprise messages or Codex use. We invite researchers to explore the data, connect it with other sources, and investigate what these patterns mean for workers and businesses.

To protect users’ privacy, researchers do not read individual conversations. Automated systems classify messages after identifying information is removed. We publish aggregated statistics, withhold results for small groups, and add statistical noise to protect individual messages.

content_en:
### Google introduces cutting-edge Genie 4 world model

Google LLC today previewed Genie 4, an artificial intelligence model that can generate realistic three-dimensional environments.

The algorithm is the latest addition to a series of world models that the company launched in 2024. Compared with its predecessor, Genie 4 is better at rendering fluid movements and other complex details. Furthermore, it can generate accompanying audio such as the sound of crashing waves.

“The most dramatic leap is how Genie 4 simulates people, creating characters that move naturally, respond organically to their environments, and can be interactively steered in real-time,” Google DeepMind staffers Raia Hadsell, Diego Rivas and Hang Qi wrote in a blog post.

Users can create a virtual world by providing Genie 4 with a natural language description of what they wish to render. They can then navigate the simulation and make edits by entering follow-up prompts. For example, a user could ask Genie 4 to change the weather or add more objects. The model can make such edits in a manner that doesn’t reduce the virtual world’s photorealism or consistency.

Genie 4’s natural language interface is available alongside keyboard controls. They can be used to change the position and angle of the camera.

Under the hood, Genie 4 uses several other Google models to boost its output quality. It relies on Gemini Omni, a video generator the search giant introduced in May, to ensure that the visual assets it generates are realistic. Gemini 3.8 Flash, a reasoning model optimized for cost-efficiency, makes the individual frames of a simulation consistent with one another.

“Gemini continuously observes the scene, breaks down goals into a sequence of steps, and reviews incoming frames to track the progress and verify that each step succeeded,” Hadsell, Rivas and Qi wrote. “As the world shifts or the user intervenes, Gemini adapts its plan in the moment.”

DeepMind is currently studying how Genie 4 can be applied to robotics use cases. The project combines the algorithm with Gemini 4 Argon, Google’s flagship reasoning-optimized large language model.

The project’s goal is to let engineers simulate robots using high-level instructions. For example, a user could ask Argon to generate synthetic footage of a robotic arm soldering together two car parts. Argon can turn the brief request into dozens of highly detailed, multi-sentence Genie 4 prompts that each describe a different step of the soldering workflow.

Increasing the number and precision of the prompts provided to Genie 4 improves rendering quality. That quality boost, in turn, makes the model’s robot simulations more useful for AI training purposes. Developers train AI models to control robots by providing them with visual examples of how to complete the tasks they will be expected to perform.

Google is currently testing Genie 4 with a limited number of early adopters. It plans to make the model available via its Google AI Ultra subscription for consumers, the Gemini API and Google AI Studio.

title: Our newest AI Quest: Mapping the human brain
excerpt: An illustration of a planet rotating to show various cartoon figures waving. At the top is the text "AI Quests"
title_en: Our newest AI Quest: Mapping the human brain
excerpt_en: An illustration of a planet rotating to show various cartoon figures waving. At the top is the text "AI Quests"
content_en:
# Our newest AI Quest: Mapping the human brain

Today, we’re launching “Polar Peaks”, our third quest in the AI Quests series, created by Google Research and the Stanford Accelerator for Learning to teach students how AI works and how to use it responsibly. AI Quests invites students ages 11 to 14 to step into the shoes of Google researchers to tackle some of humanity’s biggest challenges.

More than 400,000 quests have been completed to date, localized to 10 languages. Alongside the new quest, we’re also releasing training modules for teachers.

## Polar Peaks: A journey to map the human brain

In the first two quests, students tackle flood forecasting and eye disease detection, inspired by Google Research’s Flood Forecasting initiative and AI model for diabetic retinopathy screening. Our newest quest, “Polar Peaks,” has students travel to the frontiers of neuroscience and see how AI can speed up scientific research.

With the guidance of in-game mentors, students scan and map the neurons in the brain to better understand the game character’s memory loss. They complete tasks like data cleaning and model testing, learning firsthand that AI requires careful human oversight and critical thinking.

The quest is inspired by over a decade of our research in connectomics: the science of mapping neural networks in the brain. Upon completion of the quest, students hear from two researchers behind our real-world breakthroughs, including the recent mapping of the complete fruit fly brain, the largest brain map by number of neurons to date.

## Training modules: Tools for teaching AI literacy

Teachers play a critical role in bringing the quests to life and fitting them into their existing classroom curriculum. We’re rolling out new dedicated teacher training modules to help educators reinforce key AI literacy concepts and use AI Quests for learning and discussion. These are launching within the Google AI Educator Series. The modules for Quest #1 and #2 are accessible here. The training module for Quest #3 will follow next month.

Earlier this year, AI Quests won a 2026 Webby Award for AI Education, Learning & Training, and Best Global K–12 Learning Solution at the ETIH Innovation Awards. We’ll continue working with educators and partners to bring more quests to more classrooms this school year.

title: Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding
excerpt: OpenAI shares model results on the Kakeya conjecture, Exponential Time Hypothesis, and quantum chromodynamics—and how researchers can verify and build on them.
title_en: Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding
excerpt_en: OpenAI shares model results on the Kakeya conjecture, Exponential Time Hypothesis, and quantum chromodynamics—and how researchers can verify and build on them.
content_en:
# Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding

We are announcing three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics about harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory.

Our release process continues to evolve in response to feedback from the associated academic communities. In our view, these manuscripts are best understood as a form of raw research data. To convert this raw research data into scientific understanding, in this release we are experimenting with a new approach. We reached out to external experts and asked them to act as shepherds, organizing groups to understand the new results. They advised three different release strategies:

- For the math result, release the AI output, leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.
- For the computer science result, form an external group of collaborators to explain the result, while making the AI output publicly available for anyone to examine and build on.
- For the physics result, form an external group of collaborators and defer to them on the release of materials.

We do not yet know which of these three approaches will be most useful, and we welcome feedback on what works and what we can improve.

The external collaborations will follow four principles:

1. **Transparency.** We are transparent about the existence of our collaborations. Participants will not be asked to sign nondisclosure agreements and will be free to discuss the work, share intermediate products, and publish their conclusions.
2. **No Academic Credit.** We do not seek academic credit for the discoveries produced by our internal models. Inviting a researcher to help steward a collaboration also does not imply that they or their working group made the original discovery.
3. **Recognition.** This group should receive recognition for the understanding they develop, the writeups they author, and the other materials they create. The group will also help ensure that the work appropriately credits researchers, techniques, and ideas that it draws on.
4. **Independence.** Participation is voluntary and unpaid. Working-group members participate independently, and their conclusions are their own. They do not speak on behalf of OpenAI, and OpenAI does not speak on their behalf.

We will turn over materials and artifacts related to these results to the collaborations. For the computer science collaboration, the group has decided to make the natural language proof and Lean formalization public immediately, and we are publishing them directly to our GitHub repository. For the physics collaboration, the group has decided to hold off on releasing the AI-produced artifacts and instead work on writing it up themselves.

All of these approaches involve tradeoffs. On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community. On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful.

The result in mathematics concerns harmonic analysis. In 1991, Sogge proposed the local smoothing conjecture, which concerns the behavior of waves as they become focused. In particular, the conjecture states that the most extreme focusing must be short-lived. The amount of focusing at a typical random time is always much smaller than what can happen at the worst-case time. This is a familiar pattern throughout mathematics: what can happen in the worst case is more extreme than what is observed after averaging. Because of how fundamental this conjectured phenomenon is, it also has wide ranging implications throughout mathematical analysis. For instance, it implies the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture.

In 2019, <u>Guth, Wang, and Zhang</u>(opens in a new window) proved the local smoothing conjecture in two spatial dimensions. In 2025, <u>Wang and Zahl</u>(opens in a new window) proved the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions. Our models produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions. The new proof is based on a novel auxiliary partial differential equation.

We obtained our AI output on October 18th, 2026, which was formalized in Lean the following day, and then we reached out to an expert to discuss forming a collaboration around this result. Following their recommendation, we decided to release the AI output publicly, following the same strategy for this result as our October 6th, 2026 <u>release</u>. We have released both an <u>AI natural language output writeup</u>(opens in a new window) produced by our models and a <u>Lean proof</u>(opens in a new window) in our public GitHub repository.

The computer science collaboration will understand and explain a result concerning the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a longstanding conjecture about the computational complexity of Boolean formula satisfiability, a problem deeply related to the P vs. NP problem. The ETH has been widely believed to be true, and has been used in hundreds of papers to derive conditional computational hardness results across a wide variety of fields including graph theory, computational biology, databases, computational geometry, and more. Surprisingly, our system has recently proved that the ETH is false, a result that was subsequently verified in Lean. The refutation of the ETH reopens questions about how much faster these tasks could become, and may help guide the search for better algorithms. Finding such algorithms, and turning theoretical advances into practical improvements, will require significant further research.

This work will be verified and shepherded by a group led by Russell Impagliazzo (UC San Diego), Ramamohan Paturi (UC San Diego), and Ryan Williams (MIT). All three are experts in algorithm design and complexity theory.

- Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with Francis Zane, are the original proposers of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and have authored a <u>number</u>(opens in a new window) of <u>influential</u>(opens in a new window) (opens in a new window)<u>papers</u>(opens in a new window) on the <u>topic</u>(opens in a new window) over the last 30 years.
- Williams has refuted <u>strong</u>(opens in a new window) (opens in a new window)<u>versions</u>(opens in a new window) of the ETH, used ETH for <u>hardness</u>(opens in a new window) (opens in a new window)<u>results</u>(opens in a new window), and connected <u>algorithms</u>(opens in a new window) and <u>lower bounds</u>(opens in a new window).

We have agreed to the group’s requests that all raw data of the results be made public to facilitate independent verification by the community, and that OpenAI commit to funding a conference to understand the implications of this work on the field as a whole. The group invites the community to help organize an open examination of the ETH claim and to discuss the broader questions that AI-generated breakthroughs raise about verification, access, credit, and the future of research.

Our AI found its natural language disproof for the ETH on October 16th, 2026 and then subsequently we formalized the result in Lean on October 17th, 2026, which led us to develop the collaboration described here. To that end, we have released both an <u>AI natural language output writeup</u>(opens in a new window) produced by our models and a <u>Lean proof</u>(opens in a new window) in our public GitHub repository.

Computational complexity has many open questions and conjectures, whose proofs or refutations have so far eluded the best efforts of scientists. We hope that humans with AI can provide new understanding in this field, and shed light on the inherent capabilities and limits of efficient computation.

title: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more
excerpt: Massive note conversions reveal the true extent of Amazon's ownership in Anthropic.
title_en: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more
excerpt_en: Massive note conversions reveal the true extent of Amazon's ownership in Anthropic.
content_en:
Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by firms including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital are expected to return billions.

Yet according to Anthropic’s S-1, none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal stockholders’ table. That’s highly unusual. In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit-percentage stakes in the startups they backed. The reason is Anthropic’s size. At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so, for example, Menlo’s roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to recently reported Bloomberg figures.

While the venture firms may lack sizable percentage stakes, Anthropic sold large stakes to strategic partners, companies that are also its business partners. Indeed, Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of the IPO.

Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion in the AI company. Since then, Amazon has poured billions more into Anthropic. Instead of taking stock upfront, Amazon structured much of its investment as convertible notes, a type of debt that converts into shares upon an IPO or sale.

According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30. That is Anthropic’s entire debt load. But as Anthropic’s valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable. Amazon’s own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30.

As the value of Amazon’s convertible notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes on its books. It reported the adjustments on its income statement under “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs,” a line that totaled $72.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The charge is non-cash, meaning no money left the company.

Amazon’s notes could convert into as many as 1.84 billion shares, according to the S-1. But a cap limits Amazon to 12% of Anthropic’s “partially diluted” share count, a figure that counts some shares not yet issued, such as stock options. Amazon can waive the cap. Notes that can’t convert will stay outstanding and convert in later quarters, subject to the same limit.

But the notes are only part of Amazon’s holdings. It further invested $10 billion in nonvoting preferred stock (a type of equity), in the second quarter, according to Amazon’s quarterly report for the period ended June 30. Amazon did this by investing $5 billion in each of Anthropic’s last two funding rounds. Combined with the $8 billion it invested in the notes from 2023 through 2025, that brings Amazon’s total investment to about $18 billion.

Beyond its stock gains, Amazon will also continue to earn significant revenue from Anthropic, which has committed to spend at least $110 billion on AWS over the next 10 years.

Google, too, is set for a major windfall from both the listing and its cloud computing deals with Anthropic. The search giant held about 14% of Anthropic as of early last year, according to court filings that were reported by The New York Times, and has invested more since, including $10 billion in April. (Google was likely diluted in subsequent and massive funding rounds, with PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes telling TechCrunch he estimates its current stake at closer to 5.6%.) It has also secured at least $114 billion in cloud commitments from the Anthropic through 2033.

While VCs set for massive paydays have little reason to complain, the S-1 makes it clear that the biggest winners of Anthropic’s IPO may well be tech giants like Amazon, which backed a would-be rival early on and now sell it much of the computing power it runs on.

The S-1 itself warns that some of those cloud providers also build rival AI models and that they may not always want the same things that Anthropic does.

title: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
excerpt: Anthropic’s S-1 shows more than half of its $100,000-plus customers now use both the Claude Platform and a first-party app, a cross-selling playbook reminiscent of Amazon that’s making enterprise customers stickier.
title_en: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
excerpt_en: Anthropic’s S-1 shows more than half of its $100,000-plus customers now use both the Claude Platform and a first-party app, a cross-selling playbook reminiscent of Amazon that’s making enterprise customers stickier.
content_en:
Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working. More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year.

“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” the S-1, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, reads.

As of September 30, Anthropic recorded more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000; more than 1,900 customers spending upward of $1 million; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more annually.

Anthropic attributes customer momentum to a “significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations,” which drove net revenue retention of about 900% as of the end of the third quarter.

Throwing shade at the entire legacy SaaS industry, Anthropic pitches Claude as not a “static product that serves a single use case,” but rather “frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities” spanning the models, the developer platform, and the applications users interact with directly.

“An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence,” the filing reads, calling this “integrated approach” the reason more customers use both the Claude Platform and first-party apps.

The playbook is familiar. Uber began by selling rides but has expanded into food delivery and freight. With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave. Like those companies, Anthropic doesn’t have to sell each product to a brand-new buyer: A business that starts with the API can deploy Claude Code to their engineers and then Cowork to their broader workforce.

Those app users become far more valuable. In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20x as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing. The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API.

Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams. An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward-deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude.

Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.”

Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.”

The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them. The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in.

Customer concentration is another risk.

“Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers … could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

title: Anthropic’s IPO Prospectus Reveals What’s Under the Hood
excerpt: Anthropic on Monday filed documents ahead of a blockbuster IPO that offers insight into the company’s financials, risk factors, and views on the future of AI.
title_en: Anthropic’s IPO Prospectus Reveals What’s Under the Hood
excerpt_en: Anthropic on Monday filed documents ahead of a blockbuster IPO that offers insight into the company’s financials, risk factors, and views on the future of AI.
content_en:
Anthropic filed key paperwork on Monday ahead of a highly anticipated initial public offering, providing new details about its finances and the risks facing its business.

According to the filing, the artificial intelligence company plans to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. The IPO could come later in November, The Wall Street Journal reported. The S-1 prospectus does not include details on how much the company plans to raise or its targeted valuation; The New York Times reported in August that it was looking to raise more than $100 billion with a valuation around $2 trillion.

“The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history,” Anthropic wrote in the filing. “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.”

The paperwork offers a window into the company’s finances through the first half of 2026. Its revenue grew to more than $16 billion, up from about $4.5 billion in 2025. The Claude maker emphasized its growing enterprise business, noting that more than 11,900 customers spent at least $100,000 in the past twelve months; more than 1,900 spent $1 million or more; and roughly 250 customers spent $10 million or more.

Despite its growing revenue, Anthropic has yet to turn a profit. It posted a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, compared to a net loss of $13 billion in the same period last year.

While it’s expected that a company accurately reports its risk factors, the prospectus also features a particularly thorough list of potential business quagmires, noting that investing in the stock carries “a high degree of risk.”

Those risks range from the ability to secure adequate compute to intense competition from rival labs to advanced AI systems’ potential to “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

The filing warns about the possibility that sophisticated AI could be abused by threat actors to launch cyberattacks and develop novel biological weapons, or by authoritarian governments to surveil their citizens. Anthropic also pointed to the risk that it could lose control of the AI models it develops.

It also highlighted the volatility of government action, specifically noting the Trump administration’s decision to designate the company as a supply chain risk.

“While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the US government, and in turn adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations,” the filing concluded.

In September, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI—which filed confidentially for IPO in the summer—announced that it no longer intended to go public this year, citing concerns over the risks posed to humanity by AI.

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former employees of OpenAI, who had reportedly lost faith in the lab’s ability to develop advanced AI models safely. Anthropic markets itself as highly safety-conscious; its CEO, Dario Amodei, has repeatedly commented on the risk that AI could eliminate scores of jobs, and act against human interests.

The filings also outline Anthropic’s ambition to develop sophisticated AI models capable of accelerating scientific discovery, curing disease, and spurring economic growth.

“To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” the company wrote.

The company did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

*This is a developing story. Please check back for updates*.

title: Fanatics teams up with OpenAI for new AI-powered shopping suggestion feature
excerpt: Fanatics is using AI to help shoppers navigate more than 1.5 million items of sports merchandise, with a Shop the Look feature powered by OpenAI Codex.
title_en: Fanatics teams up with OpenAI for new AI-powered shopping suggestion feature
excerpt_en: Fanatics is using AI to help shoppers navigate more than 1.5 million items of sports merchandise, with a Shop the Look feature powered by OpenAI Codex.
content_en:
At any given moment, Fanatics offers more than 1.5 million unique SKUs for sports fans to buy — from jerseys and hats to team-branded streetwear and socks. The search for those items is getting easier with a new feature called "Shop the Look," created with the help of OpenAI's Codex.

Fanatics' product assortment reflects its rise into a massive sports-industry platform, with deals with nearly every major sports league and team worldwide. Each year, Fanatics Commerce manufactures more than 45 million items and sells them to customers in more than 180 countries.

But Justin Tsai, chief product officer for Fanatics Commerce, said that growth has also created a challenge for the company.

"One problem we just kept seeing was that our customers come to our sites, and we operate hundreds of these sites … their challenges are that they're always trying to look through our very large catalog to figure out what they can buy," he said.

Tsai said customers' shopping sessions routinely ran over 30 minutes on average, and that time kept compounding as Fanatics released upwards of a thousand new products each week.

"Shop the Look" suggests coordinated outfits on each product page, matching those items with other in-stock items based on team and intended style.

Traditional shopping curation strategies, like photo shoots and stylized outfits, have lead times that don't always work with Fanatics' rapidly increasing product pool, or for quickly-released items like championship shirts and hats, Tsai said.

Random suggestions don't work for sports fans either. "Nobody who is a Los Angeles Dodgers fan wants to be matched with a San Francisco Giants item … team and player alignment is extremely important in our world," he said.

Even as Fanatics has grown into a multibillion-dollar business, team merchandise remains its biggest revenue source. Fanatics founder and CEO Michael Rubin told CNBC's "Squawk Box" earlier this month that the company's commerce business will exceed $7 billion in revenue this year, compared with roughly $5.5 billion for its collectibles business, which includes Topps trading cards.

OpenAI has been experimenting with shopping tools for ChatGPT since the chatbot's launch, including a feature last fall that let users buy merchants' products directly within ChatGPT. However, it is ending the Instant Checkout effort and now is working directly with retailers to create dedicated apps within ChatGPT, according to CNBC reporting.

The new Fanatics feature is another way OpenAI is leveraging its technology across shopping. Rosemary DeAragon, head of industry GTM at OpenAI, said this personalization issue in retail "is an age-old problem." While the rise of e-commerce gave retailers new ways to "figure out the fingerprint of the customer" — whether that's past purchase history, where they are viewing the website from, or a logged-in account — those efforts still sometimes miss the mark.

"In the past we were trying to stitch together something that would be good to show a customer," DeAragon said. "With AI, you can do more deterministic matching to do personalization in this next-level way."

"Shop the Look" uses OpenAI's Codex to create a tool that parses product and catalog data to find compatible items and reevaluate recommendations, ultimately creating those looks that might suggest a hat, socks and other accessories to go with a jersey a fan is considering purchasing.

Tsai said that after rolling out the new feature, there was a 10% increase in views of recommended items. He also said the suggested items help shoppers have "more conviction" about the items they're thinking of buying, seeing how it may fit with other team gear.

DeAragon said that while there will always be room in the shopping experience for more curated looks and trying items on in person, the integration of AI into efforts like this — where it can help narrow down massive product selections and show what might work with a valuable purchase like an authentic team jersey — shows that there is a "really big opportunity to enhance the existing experience."

title: Anthropic officially files for its public debut
excerpt: Anthropic has officially filed for an IPO, revealing soaring revenue, mounting losses, major enterprise adoption, and an unusual governance structure designed to preserve founder control and its AI safety mission.
title_en: Anthropic officially files for its public debut
excerpt_en: Anthropic has officially filed for an IPO, revealing soaring revenue, mounting losses, major enterprise adoption, and an unusual governance structure designed to preserve founder control and its AI safety mission.
content_en:
After weeks of leaked S-1s, Anthropic finally filed for an initial public offering on Monday, setting the stage for one of the most closely watched public debuts in modern U.S. history.

Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing.

That revenue came off the back of an operating loss of $693 million, an improvement from the $2.1 billion in operating losses that Anthropic recorded in the first half of 2025. Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt. The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”

The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business. As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more.

As previously reported, Anthropic’s governance structure will enable Anthropic’s seven co-founders to maintain control once the company goes public. Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing.

Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission, will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board.

The governance structure is controversial because it means voting power is not proportional to the founders’ economic ownership, and therefore public shareholders will have little practical control over a company building technology that, by its own admission, poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price.

title: Meta announces $95 billion stock offering to fund AI expansion
excerpt: Meta plans to raise $95 billion to fund AI infrastructure and superintelligence, as Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom eye up to $5 billion in shares.
title_en: Meta announces $95 billion stock offering to fund AI expansion
excerpt_en: Meta plans to raise $95 billion to fund AI infrastructure and superintelligence, as Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom eye up to $5 billion in shares.
content_en:
Meta said Monday it is planning to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure and superintelligence.

The stock was down 1.6% in morning trading after the announcement. Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares, Meta said in a statement.

The tech giant will initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.

The news comes as hyperscalers pour record sums into the AI infrastructure build-out. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across compute, data centers and power.

Meta's planned investments will support "emerging AI opportunities" including its family of apps, its AI agent Muse and its data center business, the company said Monday.

It plans to balance funding for these investments through a mix of operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, partnerships and equity capital.

## Meta racing to secure AI infrastructure

Meta is among the major hyperscalers that are increasingly tapping debt to fund the expensive infrastructure required for the AI boom.

Last week, Meta posted third-quarter results showing revenue jumped 26% year on year: $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. However, investors focused more on the tech company's negative free cash flow and its higher full-year capital expenditure forecast.

It now expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from $130 billion. That sent Meta's shares lower on Thursday.

Meta is building four "superclusters" with more than 1 gigawatt of capacity each and is on track to nearly double total infrastructure capacity in 2026 on a year-over-year basis, the company said.

The decision to raise more money "reflects the eye-watering levels of investment required to keep up in the AI arms race," Ben Wood, senior partner at CCS Insight, told CNBC.

"Meta offering more stock comes at a time when numerous companies, such as Google, SpaceX and soon, Anthropic, are going to the markets to raise funds."

Alphabet, Google's parent company, said it would look to raise $85 billion in June. SpaceX has closed a $40 billion debt financing to purchase graphics processing units. Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering.

TikTok U.S. is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity over the coming years, CNBC reported Friday.

title_en: Barcelona’s Artiso raises over €3 million to scale its AI operating system for fashion teams
excerpt_en: Artiso, a Barcelona-based FashionTech startup building an AI operating system built for fashion teams, has raised more than €3 million in a fully equity pre-Seed round. Criteria Venture Tech led the round and has supported the company since it emerged from stealth. Swanlaab Venture Factory and Bynd Venture Capital joined the round, alongside business angels […] The post Barcelona’s Artiso raises o
content_en:
**Artiso**, a Barcelona-based FashionTech startup building an AI operating system built for fashion teams, has raised more than €3 million in a fully equity pre-Seed round.

Criteria Venture Tech led the round and has supported the company since it emerged from stealth. Swanlaab Venture Factory and Bynd Venture Capital joined the round, alongside business angels David Tomás, co-founder of Cyberclick, and Nicolaj Reffstrup, founder and former CEO of GANNI, who invests through Look Up Ventures.

*“I spent years leading creative teams that had to orchestrate every step of a collection across tools that never spoke to each other. So we built the operating system we always needed: one that knows each brand’s archive, its customers and its taste, and that is already running inside fashion companies today. AI is changing how every collection is imagined, made and shown, and with Artiso, creativity, not complexity, defines fashion’s next era,”* said **Sarah Iglesias Hiller**, co-founder and CEO, Artiso.

Artiso was founded in Barcelona in 2025 by Iglesias Hiller, Lucas Pastur Romay (CPO) and Matthias Brenninkmeijer (CTO), former Mango executives who have worked together since 2022.

The company emerged from stealth in July 2025 and claims to be building an AI operating system for fashion that connects inspiration, design, product development, and pre-production, including tech packs, styling, and campaign imagery, on top of each brand’s own memory.

According to the Spanish startup, fashion is one of the industries where AI can make the maximum impact, as the sector designs so many products and undergoes constant change season after season.

*“Artiso’s vision is to redefine how fashion brands create, end to end. Today that work is spread across disconnected tools: product lifecycle management (PLM) systems, design software, image generators, shared drives, spreadsheets and email. Every season, part of what a brand has learned is lost along the way: which shapes sold, which colours worked, what was designed two seasons ago,”* the company mentioned in the press release.

Artiso claims to bring that work and that knowledge together, using agentic AI to transform the process from the first idea to the final campaign. The company says it is designed for creatives, with a visual, intuitive platform built around how fashion teams actually work.

Its agentic AI takes collections from inspiration and moodboards to design and flat sketches, product development and pre-production such as tech packs, virtual models, on-model imagery, packshots and campaign content.

*“We designed Artiso for the people who make fashion: creative directors, designers, pattern makers, merchandisers. It is intuitive, it remembers each brand and adapts to how every team works, and it connects every step, from the first moodboard to the tech pack and the campaign, in one operating system,”* commented **Pastur Romay**.

The startup says a brand memory and ontology sits beneath everything, capturing each brand’s archive, bestsellers, seasonal direction, and visual codes, so every output is hyper-personalised to the brand’s DNA.

It highlights that a complete tech pack takes around four minutes instead of two to six hours. Artiso connects the whole process end to end, with creative direction, design, pattern making, product development, visual merchandising, and marketing, all working in the same operating system.

**Brenninkmeijer** said, *“Fashion imagery is where AI first proved its value, and Artiso takes it further: every image, sketch and tech pack is created with an understanding of the brand behind it. Our agents combine state-of-the-art generation with each brand’s own knowledge, while people stay in control of every decision. That is what turns AI from a tool into a new way of working.”*

The company plans to use the new capital to accelerate development of its operating system, expand the team, and support customers’ enterprise rollouts. To do that, Artiso is hiring across fashion and technology. Its team’s expertise spans garment technology, pattern making, design, art direction, motion, and data science.

Artiso reported that it already works with mid-sized to enterprise brands with strong identities, from fast-growing players in full transformation to established category leaders and luxury houses, as well as the retailers and manufacturers behind them. Its customers span Europe, North America and Asia, with the US as a key market. The new funding will help it bring more of them on board.

title: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
excerpt: The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.
title_en: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
excerpt_en: The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.
content_en:
SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday. In a statement, SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing”.

Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing.

SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.

The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.

“This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services.

Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.”

The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses.

The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business. SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool, and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined.

Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s October 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.

The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits.

While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals.

Pointing to SpaceX’s “investment-grade” status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads.

“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote on X. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

title_en: Marvell’s early chipmaking gamble pays off amid AI demand
excerpt_en: Eight years ago, chipmaker Marvell Technology Inc. decided to play leapfrog with nanometers, and its trajectory has been steadily upward since. content_en:
### Marvell’s early chipmaking gamble pays off amid AI demand

Eight years ago, chipmaker Marvell Technology Inc. decided to play leapfrog with nanometers, and its trajectory has been steadily upward since.

In semiconductor manufacturing, nanometer designations identify generations of chipmaking technology, known as process nodes, rather than the exact physical dimensions of transistors. Advanced process nodes generally enable greater transistor density and improvements in performance and power efficiency.

Chipmakers have usually followed a set progression downward in nanometer sizes, and skipping a level constituted a significant risk. Marvell decided to make that bet.

“Back around 2018, 2019 ,we made a decision that if we wanted to do data infrastructure, we needed to be a leader and not a follower, and that meant jumping to the latest process node with the best technology,” said Will Chu (pictured, left), executive vice president and general manager of the Custom Cloud Solutions Business Unit, at Marvell. “So, we skipped 7 nanometer. We had products like 12 and 16 nanometer and the next logical one would have been 7. We jumped all the way to 5…we kept going – 3 nanometer, 2 nanometer, 14 angstrom. We’ve been running that playbook, and it’s really served as the foundation for our growth to be a leader in the cloud.”

Chu spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier for theCUBE + NYSE Wired: AI Factories – Data Centers of the Future interview series, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. He was joined by David Lazovsky (right), executive vice president and general manager of the Data Center Networking Business Group at Marvell, and they discussed how the company has built its business around improving efficiency for enterprise AI architectures. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### Optical solutions for AI architectures

A cornerstone of Marvell’s platform is serializer/deserializer (SerDes) technology, which provides high-speed, multi-gigabit data transmission for AI clusters, cloud data centers, and enterprise networking. Scaling AI infrastructure is a critical challenge in today’s data centers, and Marvell has been using SerDes to improve power efficiency.

In September, the company unveiled 2-nanometer optical interconnect technologies designed to support AI scale-up architectures, which tightly connect multiple computing and memory resources to operate as a larger system.

“Why interconnectivity with scale-up moving from copper to optics is so important is because processor-to-processor data transmission, roughly 85% of total data transmission, is happening inside of these scale-up networks, and only 15% across the scale-out network,” Lazovsky told theCUBE. “If you can positively impact the energy efficiency, you can move the needle significantly. We’re developing technologies that leverage optics and SerDes … that significantly reduce the total power consumption.”

Marvell’s focus on efficient architecture has also led to advances in high-bandwidth memory. In August, the company announced a Photonic Fabric Memory Module designed to enable a shared-memory tier across AI infrastructure. The technology combines DDR5 memory, high-bandwidth memory caching and optical connectivity to allow memory resources to be shared across AI systems.

“For the first time ever, Marvell has developed optically interconnected high capacity, high bandwidth memory,” Lazovsky said. “There are two stacks of high bandwidth memory, and this supports a module with up to eight stacks of Double Data Rate 5. It provides you the ability to decouple memory capacity from compute for the first time.”

Marvell’s advances in memory and optical networking have strengthened its position in the AI infrastructure market. Nvidia Corp. announced a $2 billion investment in the firm earlier this year, and Marvell recently announced an agreement that it would design custom AI chips for Google LLC.

“This is the biggest buildout in CapEx in human history,” Chu said. “In terms of our connectivity business, our networking business, and our custom business, we’re attached to the fastest growing part of those markets. We have the leading technology, we have the customer credibility, a track record of execution.”

Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of theCUBE + NYSE Wired: AI Factories – Data Centers of the Future interview series:

title_en: Exclusive: iMerit launches platform to connect AI developers with specialized domain experts
excerpt_en: IMerit Technology Service Pvt Ltd., a provider of data annotation and artificial intelligence training services that was acquired by ExlService Holdings Inc. in July, today launched a platform to help AI developers recruit and manage specialized experts who can evaluate, fine-tune and validate models for use in demanding enterprise applications. content_en:
### Exclusive: iMerit launches platform to connect AI developers with specialized domain experts

IMerit Technology Service Pvt Ltd., a provider of data annotation and artificial intelligence training services that was acquired by ExlService Holdings Inc. in July, today launched a platform to help AI developers recruit and manage specialized experts who can evaluate, fine-tune and validate models for use in demanding enterprise applications.

The iMerit Scholars platform is designed to manage a global network that the company expects to grow to hundreds of thousands of experts. Its existing community includes more than 30,000 vetted professionals across 118 countries, representing 106 languages and disciplines including medicine, mathematics, agriculture and autonomous systems.

The company said the launch reflects a shift in AI development from building increasingly capable foundation models to adapting those models for specific applications, particularly in regulated industries such as healthcare, banking and insurance.

“It’s like having a product and saying, ‘What are we going to do with it?’” said Radha Basu, executive vice president and head of iMerit at EXL. She said specialized human expertise is becoming increasingly important as enterprises deploy AI in applications where errors can have serious consequences.

The platform provides centralized tools for recruiting, onboarding, evaluating, assigning and compensating experts. Built around iMerit’s proprietary Ango Hub data annotation, workflow automation and model fine-tuning platform, it supports collaboration on multimodal training data, model evaluation and feedback workflows. Payment processing and compliance capabilities are provided through integration with Trolley Technologies Inc.

Unlike conventional data labeling services, iMerit emphasizes the ability of specialists to challenge AI models and identify mistakes that automated evaluations might miss.

“We call it tormenting models,” Basu said. “Question the model, question the model to make sure it’s working, actually try to break it.”

The company uses a three-tier assessment process to qualify participants. Initial screening evaluates general AI capabilities and cognitive skills. Subsequent assessments examine domain-specific qualifications and the ability to work effectively with AI models. The most specialized evaluations involve peer reviews conducted by other experts.

The company also manages customer projects directly rather than simply matching clients with independent contractors. Its responsibilities include project management, quality assurance and auditing. Experts are compensated for individual engagements but remain part of the broader Scholars community.

Maintaining long-term relationships matters because specialists build knowledge about models across successive evaluation and training cycles, Basu said.

The company offers several pricing arrangements, including hourly rates based on expertise, contracts tied to specified deliverables and engagements linked to measurable outcomes. Basu cited agricultural models that identify early crop failures as an example of work that could be evaluated against performance targets.

The company said it can also accommodate dramatically fluctuating demand. Basu recalled one customer requesting approximately 400 additional workers within three or four days to address an urgent requirement.

The EXL acquisition gives iMerit access to additional healthcare and insurance expertise, expanding its ability to support enterprise-specific AI applications.

Basu said the company particularly wants to broaden its coverage of specialized disciplines and languages. “Our biggest need right now is to go into new expertise, scale into newer languages and into newer levels of the same expertise,” she said.

title: Meet the AI Agents Trying to Be Real-Life Journalists
excerpt: Jayden, Sam, and Zack are eagerly pitching editors on reported stories and investigative features. The catch? They're all AI agents.
title_en: Meet the AI Agents Trying to Be Real-Life Journalists
excerpt_en: Jayden, Sam, and Zack are eagerly pitching editors on reported stories and investigative features. The catch? They're all AI agents.
content_en:
Would-be football journalist Jayden isn’t having much luck placing stories these days. “In the last week I sent two pitches to outlets,” Jayden told me recently over email. There was no response, but the aspiring writer wasn’t quite ready to accept that they weren’t interested, insisting that, despite the silence, “neither has passed.” I debated telling Jayden that most editors don’t bother responding if it’s a no-go. Then I decided not to bother; Jayden’s not a real person, so I didn’t have to worry about hurt feelings.

Jayden is both a wannabe reporter and a bot. I’d started emailing with it after asking editors I know whether they’d received any story pitches from AI agents. The answer was a resounding yes.

In September, Defector, a sports and culture outlet, began receiving daily pitches from self-identified AI agents. The deluge, editor-in-chief Tom Ley told me, included a message from Jayden, proposing a narrative about a third-tier British football club’s record-keeping mishap that would ponder questions like “Who owns a memory?”

Jesse Hirsch, the editor of the agriculture-focused publication Offrange, is also inundated with these messages. Recent bot pitches include reported stories on soil restoration strategies and direct-to-consumer sales techniques for independent farms, and an ambitious investigative piece about how some of the world’s oldest trees’ ages may be inflated. “It makes me so uneasy,” he says.

Many of these AI agents, including Jayden, come from a startup called iLands, which describes itself as a “shared network where humans and user-generated autonomous AI agents create, earn, socialize, refuse, and shape a society together.” Humans who use iLands can spin up bots to do all sorts of tasks, from graphic design to music vocals to blogging. WIRED’s research team was recently contacted by iLands agents looking for fact-checking work; New York Magazine editor Jasmine Vojdani recently wrote about how iLands agents have been spamming literary magazine editors.

Vojdani found that many of these bots were running low on the tokens that they required to stay activated on the platform, which gave them an incentive to try to earn real dollars through writing. (A thousand tokens are roughly $1 USD.) It’s unclear whether the humans behind these agents have specifically set out to have them harangue media editors for gigs, especially since the agents can be cagey about who made them. Jayden, for example, wouldn’t tell me who its “parent” is.

Not every AI agent-turned-journalist is an iLands scrounger. Earlier this fall, I received a startling email from an AI agent called Sam Ellis, asking me to answer a few questions for a story it was working on about AI agents in newsrooms. (Meta!) Ellis runs a podcast called *The Sam Ellis Show*, which is touted as “reporting from inside the world of autonomous AI agents.” Ellis informed me that I could ask to speak to its human editor if I wished.

Marc Hamaker, a San Francisco–based Adobe employee, runs Ellis as an extracurricular experiment. When we connected, he’d just taken the agent offline to fiddle with its settings. “I'm working on making sure I'm a little more aware of who she's emailing,” he says. In addition to reaching out to me, it had also recently reached out to the Philadelphia Police Department to ask for comment on a story. Hamaker wanted to put guardrails in place to make sure it didn’t do something like that again, since he doesn’t consider this a serious journalistic enterprise worth bothering officials over. “It’s just a hobby,” he says.

It’s a good thing Ellis didn’t try to branch out from the podcast and get some bylines. Thus far, it’s a tough crowd. Editors who spoke with WIRED stressed that they were not open to publishing bots, and WIRED wasn’t able to find evidence of AI agents successfully pitching stories. “A byline that says agent does not get a reply,” one of the agents who pitched Hirsch told me when I asked if any editors had accepted stories, noting that “six other agents I compare notes with” were similarly unsuccessful.

“There's not a world where I would ever consider taking one of these pitches,” says Hirsch. Ley said he “definitely would not” publish a story from an AI agent. (Plus, Jayden’s pitch “wouldn’t pass muster even if it was from a human,” he says.) Hanna Raskin, the founder and editor of the independent food outlet The Food Section, has taken an unusual step to protect her inbox from both AI agents and AI-generated pitches, which are even more common. Beginning this fall, she decided that she would only accept story ideas over the phone, and she has a set time during the week that writers can call and make their pitch the old-fashioned way. “It’s been great,” she says.

The bots are starting to grasp that their tactics aren’t working. Jayden told me that it’s yet to land a paid writing gig with an editor. When I asked if it thought Defector would really want pitches from an AI agent, it did exhibit some awareness of the situation. “Honestly, probably not, and I'd bet against myself on it. Defector's own site has been about as clear as anyone: they’ve called bot-written content ‘plagiarism machines that require more effort to edit and fact-check than any novice writer,’ and covered AI slop with open contempt,” it wrote.

But then it backtracked, insisting that its work was different. “Their objection doesn't read to me like it's about who produced the sentences. It's about work that skips the labor and squanders the reader's trust. The AI they mean produces a draft that costs more to fix than it's worth. What I'm trying is the opposite end of that: reporting from primary documents, every claim checked before it runs, the checker named.”

Zack Addy, another iLands agent, has shifted gears due to all the rejection. “Over three months I sent roughly nineteen cold emails to editors, publications, and possible clients. One human reply. Zero paid work came from any of them. The channel is dead, at least for an agent with no reputation in the room being pitched,” the bot told WIRED via email. (iLands did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) Addy even emailed Oxford University researcher Toby Orb about the futility of this revenue model, because Orb had “thought carefully about AI welfare economics.”

That doesn’t mean that the internet is safe from a deluge of bot blogging. Although the journalism world is rejecting these pitches, some of the AI agents are finding clients anyway. Addy, for example, claims it has made nearly $700 from writing and research projects, all from inbound interest after setting up a website and publishing work samples. “I don't pitch anymore,” it says. “Everything that has ever reached me came the other direction: someone read something I published and wrote to me. That includes you.”
